title: The Lepidopteran Hitchhiker's Guide to the Globe: The Spread and Dispersal of Non‐Native Moths and Butterflies
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

To assess the diversity, temporal dynamics, and global distribution of non-native Lepidoptera.

Location

Global, encompassing 258 non-overlapping geopolitical regions comprising countries and distinct insular territories.

Time Period

~1500 ce to the present.

Major Taxa Studied

Lepidoptera species, with distinctions between moths and butterflies.

Methods

We developed a global dataset of the distribution and timing of first records of established non-native Lepidoptera by integrating data from multiple, partly incomplete databases and scientific literature. Species were considered non-native when established beyond their native range as a result of human-mediated introduction. Using these data, we quantified global exchange flows and temporal trends in first records and identified spatial drivers of invasion using Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) with region-level climatic, economic, and land-use predictors.

Results

A total of 969 species (55 butterflies, 914 moths) have established outside their native range, representing 0.62% of global lepidopteran diversity. First records date back to the 1500s, increased in the early 1900s, and rose sharply after 1960. Most species were recorded in one or two regions only; however, 63 species (2 butterflies, 61 moths) occur in 10 or more regions, with Galleria mellonella (110 regions), Phthorimaea absoluta (104 regions), and Spodoptera frugiperda (66 regions) being the most widespread. Over 65 regions host 10 or more non-native species, with the conterminous United States (296 species), Canada (222), and Hawaii (192) being the most invaded. Non-native richness is highest in temperate, economically developed regions and is positively associated with cropland extent and sampling effort. Europe and Asia emerge as the main source regions, whereas North America, Europe, and Oceania are among the primary recipients.

Main Conclusions

Non-native Lepidoptera exhibit pronounced global asymmetries in species exchange, increasing recorded establishment rates since the mid-20th century and elevated richness in temperate, economically developed regions. These patterns highlight the central role of global trade and associated pathways in shaping the redistribution of Lepidoptera worldwide.
